title: Unauthorised Carols
short_description: A censorship simulator with a guitar. Christmas has been banned in a post-war country, but your rock band is touring anyway. Edit your lyrics past the censors, play each gig in rhythm and shape the people's opinion one carol at a time.
description:
In a grey post-war country governed by the recently elected Loyalist Party, carols are now classified as unauthorised gatherings. As the songwriter of the Sleigh Bells, the last independent rock band in the country, your job is to get the music through.

Before every concert the setlist goes to the local censor's office. Read the new regulations, remove and edit words, swap whole verses and decide which songs to hide inside harmless folk tunes. Every edit changes the people's opinion, the band's reputation and the interest of the secret police.

Then the curtain rises. Play rock versions of famous Christmas songs in a simple rhythm game, and choose in the moment whether to sing the approved lyric or the real one. The crowd reacts to every choice, and so do the officers in the back row.

Between towns, read letters from fans, smugglers and tired bureaucrats. Bring the holiday back to a frightened country, or play it safe and keep the band together until Christmas Eve.
pitch: A censorship sim where the text you edit is your own band's Christmas rock lyrics, and the rhythm game is where you decide in real time whether to sing the approved line or the forbidden one.

title: Seating Plan: 1943
short_description: A cozy strategy-flavoured logic puzzle set during the 1943 North Africa campaign of World War II. As protocol officer of a secret Allied summit, find the perfect seat for hilariously particular generals, diplomats and staff, each with pet peeves, without starting a second war at dinner.
description:
North Africa, January 1943. While tank columns fight across the desert, the Allied leaders gather at a seaside hotel to plan the next stage of World War II, and somebody has to decide where everyone sits. That somebody is you.

Every level is a seating puzzle drawn from the summit's busy days: the opening banquet, a cramped briefing room, the motorcade to the airfield, a press photograph on the hotel steps. Each guest has a portrait card listing what they need and what they cannot stand. The admiral must face the sea, the general refuses to sit below the air marshal, two interpreters must stay beside their delegations and the war correspondent cannot be within earshot of anything secret.

Drag guests into place, watch their moods change and rearrange until the whole table is satisfied. New rules arrive as the summit goes on, from blackout curtains to surprise guests. Between puzzles, short historical notes explain the real conference behind the comedy. It is a light, top-down logic game about the small human details behind the big decisions of the war.
pitch: A cozy seating-arrangement logic puzzle set at a 1943 North African Allied summit, where the strategy of the war comes down to who refuses to sit next to whom.

title: Contraband Beard
short_description: Your beard grows while you sleep. Birds nest in it. It remembers everything. And in this kingdom, beards are illegal.
description: Grow the longest beard in the land, in a kingdom where beards are against the law. Royal barbers patrol every road, and a bare chin is the only safe chin. You are an old man whose beard has a mind of its own. Every night you sleep it grows a little longer, and it seems to be alive: sparrows nest in it, it stirs when danger is near, and it remembers the places it has brushed against. By day you wander villages, forests and castle towns, ducking into haystacks whenever a barber passes; by night you find somewhere safe to sleep. You explore, you hide, you sleep, and the beard grows. A longer beard is harder to hide, but it can lift, catch and remember things a shaven chin never could. Online, players can take the role of royal barbers and hunt each other's beards across the same countryside. Play it alone as a gentle, strange story about growing old in a kingdom that has forgotten its grandfathers, or online as a game of hide and seek.
pitch: A third-person stealth and exploration sim where your growing, living beard is your progression, your tool and the contraband you must hide, with an optional online mode where players act as royal barbers hunting it.

title: Seeds of Freedom
short_description: A third-person adventure about football, board games and history in a West African village.
description: It is early 1957 and Kofi has come home from the city to his grandfather's village on the Gold Coast, weeks before the country becomes Ghana. The village football club has been invited to play an exhibition match on Independence Day, and Kofi wants a place on the team. In this relaxed third-person 3D adventure you wander the market, the cocoa farms, the mission school and the chief's courtyard, talking to neighbours, running errands and training on the red dirt pitch by the river. Football matches are quick, arcade-style kickabouts that anyone can play. In the evenings the elders gather to play Oware, and beating them at the ancient board game is the only way to earn their stories about the cocoa boom, the colonial schools and the long road to freedom. A short, gentle and educational adventure about a real moment in history, told through sport, games and the people who played them.
pitch: An educational third-person village adventure set on the eve of Ghana's independence, where you earn your place through street football and Oware matches, and winning at the board game unlocks oral history.

title: The Ashcombe Idol
short_description: Hired as consultant on a maverick director's new film about an ancient cult, a history professor finds the prop idol on set is real. Unlock its secrets in 3D match-3 action puzzles and find out whether you are filming a story or starring in one.
description:
Professor Tom Avery was hired to make a maverick director's period film look historically accurate. Then the crew moves into the real Ashcombe University, the director unveils an idol borrowed from the college museum, and the actors start forgetting their lines in favour of words none of them should know.

Explore the campus and the half-built film sets in third person, reading old expedition journals, script rewrites and letters from the museum's founders. When the idol stirs, the game becomes an action puzzle: a rotating 3D lattice of carved stones where you swap neighbours to line up three or more matching symbols, setting off chain reactions before the lattice seals itself again.

Each solved lattice unlocks new rooms, new footage and new truths. The faster you clear it, the more the director films, and the more the idol seems to be watching back.

Has Tom become the unwitting star of the film, or has he stumbled into something far older than history?
pitch: A story-driven mystery on a film set where every sealed secret is a rotating 3D match-3 lattice, so the investigation moves forward through puzzle chains instead of dialogue trees.

title: Black Door Holdings
short_description: When his wealthiest patient vanishes, a Victorian psychiatrist is left in charge of the man's oil enterprise. Grow the business of black gold from a few wells into a global empire, while the search drags you deeper into a conspiracy of darkness and madness.
description:
England, 1891. Dr. Edmund Hale's most troubled patient, the oil baron Silas Crane, disappears the night after describing a black door at the bottom of his deepest well. His will names Hale as the trustee of everything he owns.

By day you run the oil enterprise: buy new fields, hire crews and engineers, sign contracts with railway barons, invest in refineries and ride the rise and fall of crude prices to keep the shareholders loyal. By night you search for your patient in pixel-art point-and-click scenes, questioning frightened workers, reading his session notes and examining strange core samples brought up from below.

Profit and dread are bound together. The richest wells reach the deepest places, and every barrel sold buys a little more knowledge and a little less sanity. Choose which fields to open and which to seal, whom to pay and whom to silence.

Rise from reluctant trustee to oil magnate, or follow Crane into the madness waiting beneath his empire. Several endings await.
pitch: An oil-tycoon management sim and a Lovecraftian point-and-click mystery are one loop: the psychiatrist hunting his missing patient has to run the patient's oil empire, and every profitable well drills closer to the horror.

title: Bitter Remedies
short_description: Become a self-taught back-alley chemist in 1888 London and discover the darker side of chemistry. Mix dubious concoctions for strange customers, then help hunt the killer stalking the fog before your own bottles convict you.
description:
Whitechapel, autumn 1888. Your little back-alley shop sells hair tonics, miracle lotions and the occasional black-market mixture that is better not asked about. Business is fine until a bottle with your label is found beside a victim of the most feared killer in England, and a sharp-eyed detective starts dropping by every evening with polite questions.

Days are spent behind the counter. Brewing is simple, just tip one flask into another and see what happens, but every customer wants something different and you decide what you are willing to make and who you will sell it to. Watch your stock, money and reputation, because every bottle may come back as evidence.

Nights belong to the investigation. Run real Victorian chemistry tests on the samples the detective leaves with you, match handwriting in your order book and point and click through foggy streets to question regulars and suspects. Each clue can clear your name or tighten the noose, depending on what you choose to reveal. Darkly funny, gently paced and full of moral choices, it is a detective story told from the wrong side of the counter.
pitch: A Victorian murder mystery told from behind the counter of a shady chemist's shop: the bottles you sell by day are the evidence you must analyse by night, and they may convict you.

title: Good Dog, Old Games
short_description: School trips are tough for an eight-year-old who is blind, and tougher when the class leaves him locked inside a video game museum after dark. You play as his lifelong canine companion: guide him through fifty years of playable history and help him escape.
description:
First days at school are tough enough. Ollie's first class trip is to the national museum of video games, and he cannot see a single screen. He has Juno, his guide dog, and a head full of old games his dad taught him to play by sound. When the class leaves without them and the lights go out, the two of them are on their own.

You play as Juno. Every gallery is a different decade, and every exhibit still runs: dozens of playable classics, from 1970s paddle games to 1980s arcade cabinets and 1990s home consoles. Ollie holds your harness while you lead him through side-scrolling rooms, sniff out safe paths, push switches, bark warnings and work out which old machines open which doors.

Along the way, recorded interviews with designers, original sketches and design documents in each gallery tell the story of how games were made, and hide the clues you need to get out. A gentle, old-school adventure about trust, history and seeing the world differently.
pitch: An escort-puzzle adventure where a guide dog leads a blind boy through a museum of video game history after dark, and the playable retro exhibits are the locks on every door.

title: Wallcode 1920
short_description: In a frontier town in 1920, orders are written on walls. Paint codes for your squad, break the enemy's, and reach every checkpoint first.
description:
Wallcode 1920 is a realistic first-person war game where two teams paint the walls, break each other's codes and race to the checkpoints. Neither army trusts the radio, so orders are left in paint and chalk.

Every street is an arena. You carry a paint pot, a stick of chalk and a cipher notebook. Paint a symbol and your squad obeys it: wait, cross, breach. Enemy scouts paint their own, so you copy their marks, break the cipher in your notebook and paint over them to send their runners into a dead end. Hold every checkpoint before they do and the district is yours.

Between missions the story plays out as an illustrated visual novel in the signals office, where officers, couriers and a suspected traitor test your loyalty. Every run builds a new town with fresh ciphers; fall, and you begin again with what you learned and a new class unlocked: the runner, the codebreaker or the forger who can copy enemy handwriting.
pitch: A first-person war fought only through painted wall-codes: you guide your squad with symbols, crack and over-paint the enemy's chalk ciphers, and race their runners through the streets, with the story told as a visual novel between roguelite runs.

title: Prime Time Planet
short_description: A pixel-art game show adventure about one stubborn mechanic trying to win back her family's farm on live television.
description: Welcome to Prime Time Planet, the most watched game show on television. Rook, a stubborn mechanic from a mining colony, signs up to win back her family's farm, and you guide her through every episode. On stage, every challenge is a small test of timing and nerve: cross collapsing bridges, dodge spotlights and answer the host's riddles before the buzzer. Between rounds you switch to the control room, a casual strategy screen where ratings become currency: buy sponsor gear, bribe the set designers, choose which hazards to face next and which rival contestants to sabotage. Backstage, you point and click through dressing rooms, prop stores and the editing suite to find tools, allies and secrets. The show is difficult and the hosts are cruel, yet the season follows a linear story with a beginning, a twist and a finale. Every episode Rook survives adds a little more to her kit and her fan club, so a run that starts fragile ends with a contestant the whole planet roots for. Can she survive twelve episodes, win the audience, save the farm and expose the network behind the cameras?
pitch: A linear, story-driven pixel adventure in which you are both the contestant on a cruel TV game show and her backstage schemer, spending ratings on sponsors and sabotage between short skill rounds.

title: Nora Off the Page
short_description: Run through the pages of a talking pop-up book. Each chapter is read aloud and fully animated, then turns into a fast, cute runner as Nora races to catch the little aliens escaping from her bedtime story.
description: Nora Off the Page is a colorful story adventure for families. Nora's favorite pop-up book is about a crew of tiny aliens, and tonight they have decided to leave it. With every alien that escapes, the story falls apart. Each chapter starts like a voiced storybook, with animated 3D pages, words that light up as they are read and simple choices about what Nora says and where she looks next. Then the chase begins and the game becomes a bright arcade runner. Sprint across paper meadows, cardboard rooftops and the inside of a birthday cake, jump over puddles of spilled ink, slide under fences and collect stars while the runaway aliens zip ahead in their tiny saucers. Catch them and they return to the page, adding new scenes, songs and jokes to the story. Chapters are short and linear, controls are just jump and slide, and a gentle mode keeps younger players going. Funny, warm and quick, it is a story you can read and run.
pitch: A voiced, read-along pop-up storybook where each chapter turns into a cute arcade runner, chasing the runaway aliens back onto the page to rebuild the story.

title: Billy-Jo and the Martian Gallery
short_description: A kid genius, a homemade rocket and an alien art gallery haunted by ghost dogs: a cute little 1990s-style horror adventure. Explore the dark halls, find the keys, admire the artwork and get back to Earth before bedtime without getting licked.
description:
Billy-Jo is eight, a certified backyard genius, and slightly lost. His homemade rocket ship has run out of fuel on Mars, and the only building for miles is a grand gallery of Martian art, closed for the night and full of ghosts. Friendly ones. Mostly. They are dogs, and they want to lick you.

Point, click and sneak through the gallery's echoing wings in chunky 1990s pixel art. Each room hides a puzzle built from its paintings and sculptures: line up a cosmic portrait, rotate a statue, decode the brushstrokes to find the keys that unlock the next hall and the fuel cells for your rocket. Ghost pups drift between the exhibits, sniffing for you; hide behind plinths, toss a squeaky toy to distract them or zap them with your trusty toy ray gun to buy a few seconds.

Spooky but never cruel, short and replayable, it is a love letter to the shareware adventures of the early nineties, with a gallery full of dogs that just want a friend.
pitch: An early-90s shareware-style sci-fi adventure in which a backyard rocket kid gets stranded in a Martian art gallery haunted by affectionate ghost dogs, and the artworks themselves are the puzzles.

title: The Last Löyly
short_description: A surreal first-person shooter in a sauna at the end of the world. Keep the stove burning, throw steam at the cold, and shoot back the frost that crawls out of the endless night.
description:
The Last Löyly is a surreal, psychedelic first-person VR shooter set in a Finnish sauna at the end of the world. One morning the sun did not rise. The lake froze to the bottom, the forest turned to glass, and the sauna on the shore became the only warm place left.

Between attacks you run the sauna as a realistic physics simulation. Split logs, feed the stove, carry water from the ice hole and keep the stones hot. Every ladle of water on the stones releases a wave of steam that heals you and pushes the cold back.

Then the frost comes to life. Ice figures, frozen elk and whispering shapes crawl over the snow toward the light. Hold them off with an old hunting shotgun, a flare pistol and buckets of boiling water, aiming by hand in VR or with a mouse on a flat screen.

Stay in the heat too long and the steam brings psychedelic visions of the summer that is gone. Survive the long night and find out why the sun went out.
pitch: A first-person survival shooter where the base you defend is a working sauna sim: heat the stones, throw steam to heal and push back the cold, and shoot living frost at the end of the world, with psychedelic steam visions.

title: Spellbook Mixtape
short_description: A nostalgic 2D deckbuilding adventure set in a wizard academy whose worlds look like strange 1990s music videos. Build a spellbook of cards, duel odd creatures and unravel why the music professor vanished.
description:
The music professor of a floating wizard academy has gone rogue, and the songs that hold its worlds together are falling silent. As a first-year student with a battered spellbook, you set out through twenty strange worlds that look like forgotten 1990s music videos: neon highways full of space cars, chrome deserts guarded by grinning demons, and cities of giant talking heads.

Explore each world in colourful 2D pixel art, chat with its odd residents and collect clues about the professor's disappearance. When trouble starts, combat switches to turn-based card duels. Your spells are cards drawn from a deck you build yourself: fire, frost, thunder, bloom and dream schools, each with its own sound. Play cards that share a key and they layer into a song that grows more powerful each turn.

Between worlds you return to the academy to craft new spell cards, swap tracks with classmates and decorate your dorm. Light puzzles, a gentle difficulty curve and a mystery told across every world make it a cozy, nostalgic deckbuilding adventure for anyone who grew up with wizard school stories.
pitch: A wizard-school deckbuilder where every spell is a musical phrase and every world is a surreal retro-futuristic 1990s music video, so building your deck also means composing the soundtrack.

title: Starfall Over Taihoku
short_description: During the air raids of 1945 Taipei, a schoolgirl finds a crashed rocket that is not from this world. An anime sci-fi action RPG that begins in wartime and ends in space.
description: In the last summer of the war, sirens sound over Taipei almost every day. Lin Mei-hua is fourteen, and she has learned to run when the sirens start. One morning, in a crater by the river, she finds a sleek silver rocket that no army built, and a small voice inside it asking for help. Starfall Over Taihoku is a 2D anime action-adventure in two halves. On the ground, you sneak through bombed streets and shelters, gathering parts and keeping the rocket secret while helping neighbors survive the raids. Then the rocket wakes, and the story leaves the earth: pilot it in fast side-scrolling shooter stages through orbit, asteroid belts and the derelict stations of the travelers who lost it. Salvage you bring back levels up the rocket's weapons and shields, while the friends Mei-hua makes along the way unlock new skills and story paths. Every chapter is told through hand-drawn scenes and quiet conversations about family, loss and courage. The goal is to send the stranger home before the war ends, and to decide what Mei-hua will carry back down to earth.
pitch: An anime story-driven action RPG that joins a historical home-front survival story (1945 Taipei under air raids) to a space shooter, as a schoolgirl repairs and flies home an alien rocket she found in a bomb crater.

title: Bearer of the Lamp
short_description: Step inside a faithful VR reconstruction of Queen Nefertari's tomb in this asymmetric multiplayer thriller. The lamp bearer reads the painted walls to reach the burial chamber; the agile ba-bird flock hunts the bearer through the dark to seize the light and take their place.
description:
The tomb of Nefertari, great royal wife of Ramesses II, has been rebuilt in virtual reality, chamber by chamber, with its painted gods and spells restored to their original colours. Every match takes place inside it.

The Bearer plays in VR with the only lamp. Step inside at true scale, raise the light to reveal murals and hieroglyphs, and handle interactive reconstructions that explain the history, building methods and mythology behind each scene. Every scene understood opens a sealed door. When the flock attacks, focus the lamp into a beam to fend off the monsters and survive.

The Flock plays on desktop as ba-birds, the human-headed souls of ancient Egyptian belief. Agile and fast in the dark, they swoop through shafts and side passages, but the light burns them. Hunt down the Bearer from the shadows, and whoever lands the final blow takes the lamp and becomes the new Bearer.

Play solo against an AI flock, or online with friends. Between matches, an in-game museum gathers everything you have discovered.
pitch: An educational VR tomb reconstruction turned into the arena of an asymmetric hunt: the VR player has to study the real paintings to progress while desktop players, as ba-bird souls, try to steal the lamp.

title: The Last Updraft
short_description: Two estranged sisters, one last glider race across the ruined valley they grew up in. Play the story alone against your rival sibling, or split the screen with a friend and fight over every shortcut, memory and finish line in versus mode.
description:
Years after the war emptied the valley, the old glider race returns for one final season. Ada and June used to fly it together. Now they barely speak, and both of them have entered.

Every chapter is a head-to-head race between the sisters, part sport, part argument. You launch from broken towers, ride the wind through collapsed bridges and overgrown factories, and fight for the faster line. Between races, each sister explores the valley on foot, finds old letters and photographs, and solves small puzzles that open new routes: a shortcut their father built, a thermal above the dam where they once crashed.

In single-player you choose a sister and race the other, whose flying changes with what you learn about her. In versus mode, two players take a sister each in split-screen or online, and the story's ending depends on who wins the final course. A competitive sports game about family, rivalry and finally saying sorry.
pitch: A story-driven PvP sports game: the whole narrative is a head-to-head glider rivalry between two sisters, and when two players take a sister each, whoever wins the versus final decides how the story ends.

title: Secondhand Truth
short_description: Plant one whispered sentence in a medieval market town and watch it change as it passes from mouth to mouth. Steer the gossip through boasters, mishearers and zealots so the right version reaches the right ear by nightfall.
description: A small medieval market town runs on routine: the baker opens at dawn, the washerwomen meet at the river, the guards drink at the tavern after the evening bell. You are a stranger with one tool, a whispered sentence. Each chapter sets a goal, such as freeing a wrongly jailed tanner or stopping a forced marriage, and a version of the truth that must reach a particular ear before nightfall. Choose who hears your words first, then watch the day unfold in pausable real time as the sentence travels. Every listener retells it in their own way. The boaster doubles every number, the half-deaf blacksmith swaps similar-sounding words, the priest adds a moral, and the skeptic strips out the juicy part. Changes stack, so a harmless remark about a missing goat can reach the magistrate as an accusation of witchcraft. Study schedules and temperaments, intercept the story with a second whisper to correct its course, and never speak to the same person twice, or suspicion will trace the tale back to you. Each chapter has several solutions, and the outcomes carry into the next.
pitch: The unit you control is gossip itself: a sentence that mutates predictably through each townsperson's personality, turning a social network into a routing puzzle.

title: The Lip Reader
short_description: From a rented attic above a divided city, spy on conversations you can never hear. Decode lip movements frame by frame, rebuild what was said, and decide whose secrets end up in your report.
description: It is the winter of a long cold war, and your agency has given you a telephoto camera, a pair of binoculars and an attic window above a busy square full of cafes, tram stops and embassy doors. You cannot hear a single word below, but you can read lips. Each case begins with surveillance: track targets, catch them mid-conversation, and record short reels of film. Back at your desk you scrub through the footage frame by frame and match mouth shapes to sounds. Many sounds look identical on the lips, so 'bomb', 'mop' and 'pop' share a shape, and only context, gestures and what you already know can tell them apart. Assemble the fragments into a transcript, flag the uncertain words, and file your report. Your superiors act on what you write, so a single misread can burn an innocent courier or let a defector slip away. As the cases connect, you start to notice that someone in the square is choosing their words very carefully, as if they know exactly where you are watching from.
pitch: Lip-reading becomes the core deduction mechanic, where visually identical mouth shapes create real ambiguity that the player resolves through context and evidence.

title: The Quiet Meter
short_description: Solve crimes in a twelve-storey apartment block using nothing but minute-by-minute electricity, water and gas readings. Learn every appliance's signature, rebuild each resident's night, and find the reading that should not exist.
description: A building is a diary that nobody meant to write. As a forensic analyst for the city's utility company, you are called in when the police have run out of witnesses. Each case hands you a block of flats and a night's worth of meter data: electricity, water and gas, sampled every minute for every unit. At first it is just lines on a chart. Then you learn to read them. A sharp three-minute spike is a kettle. Hot water paired with a gas burner is a shower. A slow rhythmic wave is a washing machine on its spin cycle. Tag these signatures, place them on a shared timeline, and the residents come alive: who woke at three, who pretended to be away, which empty flat suddenly drew power for exactly forty minutes. Cross-reference units to catch people moving between them, test theories against the data, and submit a reconstruction that must account for every anomaly. Later buildings add solar panels, faulty wiring, shared boilers and suspects who know how to disguise their footprint.
pitch: Detective work done entirely from household utility consumption curves, turning appliance signatures into the evidence and the timeline into the solution.

title: The Interpreter's Chair
short_description: Two nations are negotiating a ceasefire, and you are the only person in the room who understands both sides. Translate faithfully, or quietly bend every sentence toward the peace you believe in, without getting caught.
description: A ceasefire summit has been arranged in a remote mountain hotel, and you are the sole interpreter between two delegations who share no common language. Every word passes through you. As each speaker talks, you hear the full meaning, including the threat hidden in a polite phrase and the concession a general did not mean to offer. Then you choose how to deliver it. Render it faithfully, soften an insult, sharpen a vague promise, drop a dangerous aside, or slip in a phrase of your own. The table reacts in real time: tempers rise and cool, trust grows or collapses, and positions on the map shift. Your manipulation is not invisible. Each side has aides who understand fragments of the other language, and a careless change can be noticed, recorded and used against you. Between sessions, corridors, dinners and late phone calls let both sides press you for private favours. Five days of talks lead to many endings, from lasting peace to renewed war to your own quiet disappearance.
pitch: The player is the communication channel itself, editing every sentence of a negotiation while partially bilingual witnesses threaten to expose the edits.

title: Sold to the Back Row
short_description: Become a fast-talking auctioneer. Keep your bid chant locked to the beat while scanning a packed room for nods, winks and twitching paddles, and squeeze every last coin from the crowd before the hammer falls.
description: Auctioneering is music with money attached, and you are about to learn the rhythm. Each lot opens with a starting price and a room full of bidders. Your chant is a rhythm track: hit the beats to keep the filler words rolling and the crowd hypnotised, and if you stumble the room loses interest. While your mouth runs, your eyes work. Bidders signal in tiny ways: a raised catalogue, a tap of the nose, a glance to a partner, a paddle lifted half an inch. Spot a bid, point at it on the beat, and the price climbs a step. Every bidder has a hidden budget and a temperament, so read their hesitation, coax them with a smaller increment, or bluff a bid from the back wall if you dare. Drop the hammer too early and you leave money on the table; wait too long and the lot goes unsold. Work your way from livestock barns and storage lockers to estate sales and glittering city galleries, then face rival auctioneers in a split-screen chant-off.
pitch: A rhythm game fused with crowd-reading, where keeping the auction chant on beat and spotting subtle bids must happen at the same time.

title: Card Section
short_description: Plan the giant pictures that thousands of fans make by holding up coloured cards, then conduct them live on match day. Late arrivals, swapped seats and distracted children will ruin your masterpiece unless you react fast.
description: Halftime is in ninety seconds and twelve thousand people are about to become your pixels. In the planning phase you design card stunts for a stadium's seating: draw a mosaic on the seat grid, break it into frames for animated sequences, and print an instruction slip for every seat. You choose how complicated each slip should be, because a clever ten-step animation means nothing if fans cannot follow it. On match day the plan meets the public. Spectators arrive late, sit in the wrong row, drop their cards, hold them upside down, or wander off for snacks just before the big reveal. You conduct from the press box in real time: call each flip over the loudspeaker, spot gaps forming in your image, send volunteers running with spare cards, and improvise simpler fallbacks when a section falls apart. Images are scored for accuracy and crowd excitement, unlocking larger venues and trickier stands. Friends can join online, each conducting their own block of seats, and a design editor lets you share stunts with the community.
pitch: An entire stadium crowd becomes an unreliable pixel display that you design for in advance and then conduct live as people fail to follow instructions.

title: Rounds and Changes
short_description: Ring tower bells the old way with friends: each player pulls one heavy swinging bell, swapping places in shifting mathematical patterns while keeping every stroke perfectly in time.
description: High in a village church tower, eight ropes hang in a circle. Each one is attached to a bell weighing as much as a small car, and each is yours to control. This kind of ringing is not about melodies. The bells sound one after another in rows, and with every row the order changes according to a pattern called a method. Your job is to know where your bell belongs in each row and get it there. Pull harder to hold the bell up longer and strike later; check your pull to come in sooner. Overdo it and the bell swings past its balance point and the whole band falls apart. Ring alone with patient computer ringers, or join up to seven friends online, each on a rope, while one of you conducts, calling out changes that rearrange the pattern mid-flow. The campaign follows a neglected tower brought back to life: recruit locals, learn new methods, ring for weddings and festivals, and train for a marathon touch of thousands of unbroken changes.
pitch: A co-op rhythm game built on the real tradition of change ringing, where the challenge is timing a heavy swinging bell while tracking your place in a moving permutation.

title: Unseen Stage
short_description: A street mime whose imaginary walls, ladders and ropes become solid, but only while someone is watching. Gather an audience, hold their attention, and perform your way across a city that has forgotten how to pretend.
description: In a grey city where nobody has time for street performers, a silent mime discovers that a convincing act becomes real. Trace a wall with your palms and it blocks the way. Climb an imaginary rope hand over hand and you rise. Lean on a counter that is not there and it holds your weight. There is one condition: the object exists only while an audience member is watching and believing. Every level is a puzzle about attention. Gather onlookers, keep them entertained, and lead them to places where their gaze covers the gaps you need to cross. Children believe almost anything, office workers glance away to check the time, and a stern critic needs a flawless performance before your ladder turns solid. Lose the crowd mid-climb and you fall. Perform gestures with precise inputs, chain them into routines, and use your invisible creations to trap guards, lift friends and cross rooftops. The wordless story, told in hand-drawn panels, follows the mime as the city slowly learns to play again.
pitch: Pantomimed objects are solid only inside an audience's line of sight, so crowd attention becomes the platforming resource the player must earn and steer.

title: Root Exchange
short_description: Become the fungus beneath an old forest and run its hidden marketplace. Thread through the soil, link tree roots, broker sugar for minerals, and take your cut while keeping the whole forest alive through drought and rivals.
description: Beneath every old forest lies a network of fungal threads linking the roots of trees, and you are that network. Trees make sugar in the sunlight but struggle to pull minerals and water from the soil; you mine minerals but cannot make sugar. Every connection you grow is a trading route. Extend threads through layers of earth, wrap the roots of oaks, pines and birches, and set exchange rates with each tree. Ferry surplus sugar from sunlit giants to shaded saplings, move water toward the thirsty in a dry spell, and skim a share from every transaction to fund further growth. The forest responds to your choices. Starve the young trees and the canopy thins within a decade; overcharge the old ones and they cut you off and court a rival fungus spreading from the next valley. Seasons shift demand, beetles and drought test your reserves, and loggers can sever whole districts overnight. When your network is strong, raise mushrooms above ground to send spores toward new forests with harsher conditions.
pitch: The player is the underground fungal network that brokers nutrients between trees, an ecological trading economy seen entirely from the soil.

title: Long Water
short_description: You are a river flowing across ten thousand years. Carve valleys, choose where silt settles, flood and retreat, and shape the towns that rise on your banks while they build dams and walls to bend you to their will.
description: Begin as meltwater at the edge of a retreating glacier and end, if you endure, as a broad delta spilling into the sea. Each turn spans a decade. Spend the strength of your current to cut into an outer bank, drop silt on an inner bend, abandon a loop to leave an oxbow lake, or gather spring rain into a flood that spreads fertile mud across the plain. Life answers your choices. Reeds, fish and herons follow clean shallows, and people follow the fish. Villages appear where your soil is richest, and they love you while you feed them. As they grow, they begin to argue with you: mills narrow your channel, embankments pin you in place, bridges ask you to stay still, and eventually a dam threatens to stop you altogether. You can bend around them, nourish them, or break them with a hundred-year flood. Every valley is procedurally shaped, and every playthrough leaves a different map of towns, wetlands and ruins along the path you chose.
pitch: The player is a river across millennia, shaping its own course while the civilizations it feeds work to pin it in place.

title: Fair or Foul
short_description: Become the weather watcher of a stormy nineteenth-century fishing village. Read clouds, pressure and seabirds each dawn, raise your forecast on the harbour mast, and live with what happens when the boats come home, or don't.
description: The fishing boats will not leave the harbour until they see your flag. As the new weather watcher of a small village on a wild northern coast in the nineteenth century, your forecast decides whether families eat this week and whether some of them come back at all. Each dawn you climb to the station and observe. The sky is fully simulated, with fronts, pressure systems and cloud formations that behave as they do in reality, so a thickening veil of high cloud, a falling barometer and a wind backing to the south all mean something. Combine your instruments with the village's own signs: gulls staying ashore, an old sailor's aching knee, a halo around the moon. Then raise a fair, caution or storm signal on the harbour mast and watch the fleet decide. Your accuracy builds trust, and trust changes behaviour, since a doubted forecaster is ignored on the day it matters most. Over the seasons, upgrade instruments, keep a logbook of patterns, trade readings with distant stations by telegraph, and get to know the people whose lives ride on your judgement.
pitch: A forecasting game where the player reads a physically simulated sky to make daily predictions whose credibility decides a village's fortunes.

title: Valley Fold
short_description: Fold your own army. Every crease you make on a square of paper decides how your units move, strike and survive, then they march into turn-based battles across a cluttered scholar's desk.
description: On a scholar's desk at night, paper armies wage war across open books, ink pools and the ridges of a fallen ruler. You do not recruit soldiers; you fold them. Each unit starts as a blank square on a crease grid. Place mountain and valley folds, collapse the sheet, and the shape you create becomes the unit. Long sharp points give reach, extra flaps become legs and speed, stacked layers turn into armour, and broad wings let a piece glide from the rim of a teacup. Simple folds are reliable; ambitious ones are powerful but tricky to collapse correctly. Then take the fight to the grid in turn-based battles where terrain matters: ink soaks and weakens paper, a desk fan scatters light units, and a candle is as deadly as it sounds. Damaged units come back creased and torn, and you can refold them between fights, but every refold weakens the sheet. Collect new papers, from thin tissue to stiff card and metal foil, as you push through a roguelite campaign across a sprawling study.
pitch: Unit design is literal paper folding: the geometry of the crease pattern you fold becomes the unit's stats in tactical combat.

title: The Last Tuning
short_description: A piano tuner is hired to restore every instrument in a shuttered mansion. Tune by ear, string by string, as each sour note you correct quiets something in the house, and each one you leave wavering draws it closer.
description: In the autumn of 1926 you are hired to tune every piano in a shuttered country house: the grand in the ballroom, the upright in the servants' hall, the toy piano in the nursery and dozens more. The family will not say why, and they will not stay the night. Tuning works the way it does in real life. Open the instrument, set your lever on a pin, and listen. Two strings slightly apart produce a wavering beat; turn the pin until the beat slows and vanishes, or until it pulses at the exact rate a tempered interval needs. Play with headphones and the house becomes an instrument too. Every piano you set right calms part of the presence that lives here and reveals a fragment of the composer who once did. Every wavering, sour note attracts it. You cannot fight it and you cannot run far, so you must decide how much noise to make, which rooms to finish first, and when to stop and simply listen. Letters, scores and old recordings slowly reveal what was left unfinished.
pitch: A horror game whose central skill is authentic by-ear piano tuning, with acoustic beating serving as both the puzzle and the thing that summons danger.

title: Morning Control
short_description: Lead the avalanche crew at a mountain resort. Dig snow pits before dawn, read the buried layers, choose which slopes to blast or close, and open the mountain safely before the first chairlift turns.
description: Every morning the mountain asks a question, and you have until the lifts open to answer it. As head of the avalanche team at a busy ski resort, you start in darkness with overnight reports: snowfall, wind direction and temperature swings that may have buried a weak layer under a fresh slab. Choose which slopes to investigate, ski out with your crew, and dig. Each snow pit is a cross-section of the season, and reading it is a puzzle of crystal shapes, hardness and test results that tell you whether a slope will hold. Then decide: throw hand charges, fire the avalanche cannon, ski-cut a slope yourself, or keep it roped off for the day. The resort manager wants the famous runs open by nine, the guests want fresh powder, and the mountain does not care about either. Through the day, sun and wind keep changing the picture, so you reopen, close and respond to rescues. Seasons build on one another, since every storm and every decision is buried in the snowpack you will dig through next month.
pitch: Snow science as the core loop: reading a layered snowpack and triggering controlled slides, with the whole season's weather persisting as buried history.

title: Altitude Only
short_description: A long-distance balloon race where your only control is up or down. Read invisible rivers of wind stacked in the sky, spend your ballast wisely, and drift hundreds of miles to the target ahead of your rivals.
description: Gas balloons have no engine, no rudder and no steering wheel. You can rise by dropping sand and sink by venting gas, and that is all. Yet the sky is layered, with each altitude carrying its own wind, and a good pilot steers by choosing which layer to ride. Before each race, study forecasts and launch small pilot balloons to see how winds turn with height. In the air, watch cloud drift, chimney smoke and other racers for clues, then commit: climb into a fast westerly, drop into a slow southerly to curve around a mountain range, or hold steady and wait for the evening shift. Every climb costs ballast and every descent costs gas, and both run out. Races cover hundreds of miles and play out over hours compressed into tense, quiet sessions, ending in a precise landing near a target. Online, everyone shares the same simulated sky, so watching another balloon swing away reveals a wind you cannot see, while simply copying a rival means you can never beat them.
pitch: A racing game with a single vertical control, where steering means reading and choosing between invisible stacked layers of wind.

title: The Night Compositor
short_description: Work the night shift at a nineteenth-century newspaper, setting every word by hand in backwards metal type. Justify lines, fit columns around adverts, and lock the front page before the presses roll at dawn.
description: It is midnight in a city newsroom in the 1890s, and tomorrow's paper does not exist yet. Stories arrive in scrawled handwriting, and you must turn them into metal. Pick letters from the type case, where every letter has its own compartment, and drop them into your composing stick, upside down and mirrored. Fill each line exactly, using thin and wide spaces to justify it, because a loose line will fall out on the press. Then lay the finished columns into the page frame, a fitting puzzle of headlines, advertisements and illustrations that must lock together without gaps. The clock never stops. Breaking news forces you to tear up a finished column, the editor wants a bigger headline, the censor sends a list of words to cut, and the type case runs short of capital letters halfway through an election story, so you have to rephrase on the fly. Each morning the printed paper shows your mistakes in public. Between shifts, hire apprentices, buy new typefaces, and follow the stories that slowly reveal what is happening in the city.
pitch: Hand-setting mirrored metal type under a deadline, combining typing, word-fitting and spatial page layout into a single job loop.
